rows.title: Monetary Policy
rows.figure: Fed Dec hike ~80–85%; ECB Dec ~89% (Nov 4); BoJ Dec ~80%; BoC Dec ~35%; RBNZ Dec <50%; BoE 4.00% and RBA 4.85% after November hikes
rows.read: A December Federal Reserve hike is still the market's main expectation, which keeps rate support under the dollar before today's US inflation figures. Bank of Japan meeting notes showed several members want to hike faster, backing the yen's case for December. Job losses in Canada and New Zealand, and gloomy Australian households, give those banks reasons to wait.

rows.title: Growth
rows.figure: China Oct imports +41.6% y/y (fcst +32%), exports +35.2%, surplus $105.3B; Westpac AU confidence 78.2; Japan Sep household spending −6.8% y/y; UK Q3 GDP Thu, fcst +0.7% q/q
rows.read: China bought far more from abroad than expected in October, a sign that demand there may be firming, which is mild good news for the Aussie and the kiwi. Australian households, though, are the gloomiest in four years, and Japanese spending is weak. The US job market still looks firmer than Canada's or New Zealand's, a split that favours the US dollar.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.figure: US Oct CPI Tue 7:30 AM CT: fcst +0.3% m/m, core +0.2% (Sep +0.6%); NY Fed 1-yr expectations 3.9%; Brent ~$91
rows.read: Oil kept falling, which eases fears that the energy shock keeps feeding prices. But Americans still expect prices to rise fast, so today's US figures decide whether the Fed feels more or less pressure. A hot reading would favour the dollar; a soft one would help gold, the euro and the yen.

rows.title: Risk Sentiment
rows.figure: S&P 500 +2.35% Mon, Nasdaq +2.7%; Nikkei +2.5%, KOSPI +4% in Asia; NZD/USD +1.56% and AUD/USD +0.80% Mon
rows.read: Stocks held their rebound from last week's AI and chip-stock slump, and hopes of calm in the Gulf kept war fears low. That keeps safe havens like the franc and the yen quiet and leaves the kiwi and the Aussie near Monday's highs. Markets are calm but waiting, since a hot US inflation reading could shake them.

rows.title: Terms of Trade
rows.figure: Brent ~$91.44, WTI ~$85.72 in Asia; Monday settles $92.57 (−5.85%) and $86.85 (−4.4%); Brent $116.72 at the Oct 30 close
rows.read: Oil kept sliding to its lowest since late August as President Trump held off on new strikes on Iran and supply looked more plentiful. That cuts the energy bill for importers like Japan and the euro area. It also takes support from the Canadian dollar, which slipped overnight.

rows.title: Positioning
rows.figure: CFTC Nov 3: hedge funds for USD, JPY, AUD, GBP; against NZD (19th percentile), CAD (21st), EUR (35th); 4-week change NZD −22K, EUR −34K contracts; real money very bearish GBP and AUD; next report Friday
rows.read: Hedge funds lean toward the dollar and the yen and against the kiwi, the Canadian dollar and the euro, and over the past month they sharply added to their bets against the kiwi and the euro. In the Aussie and the pound, hedge funds and real-money investors sit on opposite sides, with real money betting heavily against both. Monday's jump in the kiwi shows how quickly one-sided bets can unwind.

rows.title: Fiscal
rows.figure: US 10-year auction $42B Tue 12:00 PM CT; 3-year sale Mon bid-to-cover 2.53 (weakest of 2026); NZ official result Nov 27; Democrats control House and Senate
rows.read: No new budget news overnight. Weak demand at Monday's US three-year bond sale puts today's 10-year sale under watch, since soft buying keeps US borrowing costs high. A Democratic Congress still makes President Trump's spending plans harder to pass, a mild drag on the dollar.
